node.label: Bryan D. Palmer
node.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
node.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Bryan D. Palmer (b. 1951); “Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); A Culture in Conflict: Skilled Workers and Industrial Capitalism in Hamilton, Ontario, 1860–1914 (1979); The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981); with Gregory S. Kealey, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); Working-Class Experience (1983; 2nd ed. 1992); “Response to Joan Scott” (International Labor and Working-Class History, 1987); Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (1990); “Homage to Edward Thompson” (Labour/Le Travail, 1993–94); E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994). After 2000: Canada’s 1960s (2009); “Radical Reasoning” (Underhill Review, 2009). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Scott’s reply (1987); Callinicos (1992); Dissenting Traditions (2021), with essays by Rogers, McCoy and Pearson.
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay in full; the first page of his 1987 'Response to Joan Scott' (publisher's preview image) and its notes as listed by the publisher; Scott's 1987 essay (first page) and her 'A Reply to Criticism' (1987) in full; Bercuson (1981, pp. 95–97); Callinicos's 1992 review of Descent into Discourse in full; 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993–94), searched in full and read at pp. 67–68 (Part I) and 16–18 (Part II); and 'Radical Reasoning' (2009) in full. Unread here: the monographs (A Culture in Conflict, Dreaming of What Might Be, Working-Class Experience), Descent into Discourse itself (borrow-only; its words are quoted as Callinicos quotes them, with his page references), pp. 15–23 of the 1987 response (quoted only through Scott's reply and through McCoy, 2021), The Making of E. P. Thompson (1981), Objections and Oppositions (1994) and Canada's 1960s (2009). He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay presents its thesis as 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981) on working-class culture, by Scott (1987) on language and gender, and, from a sympathetic Marxist position, by Callinicos (1992). The 2009 critique of the liberal order is dated in its label and text. The essays in Dissenting Traditions (2021) are later readings and are labelled as such wherever they are cited.

proposed_edges.relationship: Craft culture and class conflict: skilled workers' culture as a resource in working-class formation, from 'Most Uncommon Common Men' (1976) to A Culture in Conflict (1979), carried on with Kealey in Dreaming of What Might Be (1982; known here only through later readings); contested by Bercuson (1981)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 5–31, read in full in the journal's PDF. Artisan radicalism 'was part and parcel of a larger context, a matrix of institutions, ideologies and traditions which, taken together, define the contours of a singular culture' (p. 7); 'in viewing culture as a resource and society as the arena in which that resource is utilized, we are necessarily led to a refinement of our conception of the "levels" at which culture operates' (p. 8); 'It has become a standard axiom of an emerging social history of the working class that the artisan, not the debased proletarian, fathered the labour movement. As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop' (p. 14), where Thompson, the Webbs, Musson and Pelling are cited as agreeing on the skilled mechanic's influence. In-period reception, from a critic: David Bercuson, 'Through the Looking Glass of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 95–112, pp. 95–97 re-read in the journal's PDF. He quotes A Culture in Conflict (his n. 10: pp. xii–xiv) for a method of 'sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past', in which 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research', and (n. 11: p. xiii) for 'a tradition of empirical Marxism' (p. 96); 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (p. 97). Bercuson's methodological objection (pp. 107–108, read in the journal's PDF): 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; he asks whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107), and writes that 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108). Kealey's companion defence in the same issue defends class analysis and culture (wcreq_kealey_1981; not re-read in 1.134). A Culture in Conflict (1979), Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992) were not read here; they are cited at title level and through Bercuson. The edge's in-period evidence covers 1976–81; the 1982 Knights of Labor book is mentioned in the relationship text but rests only on McCoy's later quotation, so the label's dates stop at 1979. Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) reads A Culture in Conflict as following Thompson in finding resistance among skilled artisans and in quoting Thompson's working-class culture as a 'way of struggle' rather than a 'way of life' (citing pp. xii, xiv); Ted McCoy (2021) quotes Kealey and Palmer's chapter on the Knights: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names Palmer with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay calls its thesis an axiom of an emerging field. edge_890 (ep_thompson → cdn_working_class) and edge_886 (marx → cdn_working_class) stay: they record the Thompsonian and Marxist resources and the 1981 debate; this edge records Palmer's own contribution.

proposed_edges.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson).

proposed_edges.relationship: Descent into Discourse: the linguistic turn in social history criticised as a 'reification of language', with class held to originate in relations of production rather than in discourse; Stedman Jones's languages of class a principal target (1987–90)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The book (Temple University Press, 1990) was not read: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and its search-inside service returned HTTP 403. Its wording is taken from an in-period review that quotes it with page numbers: Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992), pp. 311–313, read in full in the journal's PDF. Callinicos quotes Palmer: 'Much writing that appears under the designer label of poststructuralism/post modernism is, quite bluntly, crap' (199); Callinicos describes Palmer's standpoint, in his own words, as 'not that of a defensive empiricism but of a critical, anti-Stalinist Marxism', and quotes the book: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (xiii); yet discourse theory 'contains insights and guides capable of opening new doors of understanding to historians committed to a materialism that recognizes the need for a rigorous reading of documents and texts/contexts' (189). The book is 'a critical survey of "the reification of language"' from the Russian Formalists through Foucault and Derrida that 'traces the vulgarization of their ideas by historians working in the fields of politics, gender, and class' (p. 312). Against 'the reduction by Gareth Stedman Jones et al. of class as a discursive construct', Palmer writes that 'class relations are, in origin, economic relations rooted in the capitalist process of accumulation, whereby one social stratum expropriates surplus from another' (138) (p. 312). Callinicos's in-period objections: Palmer is 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received in the English-speaking world' and misreads Foucault's Archaeology (p. 312); his claim that 'class as an objective economic reality is not present before the arrival of industrial capitalism' (139) sits oddly with Ste Croix; 'Perhaps, like Edward Thompson before him, Palmer has reacted to the dissolution of agency into structure by underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action' (p. 313). He calls the results 'admirable' and his disagreements 'relatively minor' (p. 312). The target was already set in 1987: Palmer's ILWCH response (p. 14 and n. 2, read) borrows phrases from Stedman Jones's Languages of Class for the first-person scene that opens it, and Scott's reply says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (ILWCH 32, p. 41). Later readings, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer in 1993 granting that 'Poststructurally inclined historians rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted; unread here); Finkel (2021) calls the book Palmer's 'anger with the discursive turn'. Scope: a critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of class, not of attention to language as such. edge_105 (language → social) and edge_200 (historyworkshop–language) stay.

proposed_edges.relationship: Liberal order criticised as an elastic, seemingly trans-historical category that sidesteps capitalism's changing historical structures, in a review of McKay's Reasoning Otherwise (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. 'Radical Reasoning', a feature review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009, read in full (web text; locators below are pages of the print PDF, https://www3.carleton.ca/underhillreview/09/fall/reviews/print/Palmer.pdf). He reads McKay's liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism', and says past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order."' 'As an elastic category, liberal order can contain almost anything associated with what has traditionally been understood about modern developing societies'. 'The danger in deploying liberal order in this way, as a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework, is that it actually sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'; 'it may well be impossible to discern anything distinctly Canadian about the notion of liberal order'; 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression.' He adds that McKay's 'elastic understanding of Gramsci's hegemony conflates what Gramsci differentiated as a "separation of powers"'. The elasticity and capitalism argument is at pp. 3–4 and the Gramsci criticism at pp. 4–5. Qualifications kept: 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself' (p. 4), and the book 'stands as an undeniable achievement' (p. 31). This is Palmer's interpretation of the framework. McKay's own position, recorded under lof_mckay_2009 and known here through Fecteau's quotation, distinguishes the two analytically while treating them as historically close: 'Liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated. Yet, after the 1840s, they also could not be easily separated' (p. 385, as quoted by Fecteau, 2009). That chapter appeared in the same year and is not a reply to Palmer; no direct rejoinder was found. Scope: the essay reviews Reasoning Otherwise and quotes Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005, p. 84); it does not discuss the 2000 prospectus directly. McKay's reply, if any, was not checked. The critique-audit of 2026-10-14 proposed a group edge cdn_working_class → liberal_order_framework on this text; with the person entry, the person edge carries it and the group edge is not proposed. edge_845 (karl–liberal_order_framework, comparison) stays.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson's history of class and culture as a model for Palmer's labour history and the subject of his studies of Thompson (1976–94), with disagreements Palmer stated, including on base and superstructure
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Palmer's 1976 essay (read) cites Thompson's Making for the skilled mechanic's leading role (p. 14 and notes). Bercuson (1981, p. 97, re-read): 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes."' Kealey (1981, p. 82; existing note, not re-read) cites Palmer's forthcoming book as the place where Thompson's work is analysed at length. Palmer's 1987 ILWCH response (notes as listed by the publisher) leans on Thompson: n. 8 cites The Making (pp. 529–40) for how historians have interrogated the language of sources, n. 10 says 'This unity of the political and the economic is fundamental to Thompson's Making', and n. 14 cites The Poverty of Theory (pp. 235–36). 'Homage to Edward Thompson', Labour/Le Travail 32 (1993) and 33 (1994), read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18: Palmer sets out Thompson's socialist humanism against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor' (Part I, p. 68) and quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (Part II, p. 17; Thompson's interviews, cited in n. 9, not read). Palmer's two books on Thompson, The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981) and E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994), are cited at title and imprint level only (Open Library). Stated disagreement, in period: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) notes that Descent into Discourse 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (pp. 209–11 of the book, unread here). Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer's 1993 interview in Left History: 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted; the journal's PDF was behind a bot wall); Rogers calls The Making 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation, finds Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position', but notes that 'Palmer does not necessarily agree with Thompson's reading of Marx' and 'is not a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism', since he holds to a revolutionary vanguard. Influence, not discipleship: the arrow records Thompson's work as Palmer's model and subject; it does not claim that Palmer adopted Thompson's positions whole.

verification.note: Read in full in the publisher's PDF (free access on Cambridge Core; 'Response to Controversy'). Passages used: Palmer and Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language"'; Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); Palmer quoted: 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened'; 'class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40); 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (p. 41); Palmer quoted on those 'on the left ... new_sources.title: Alex Callinicos, review of Bryan D. Palmer, Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992): 311–313.
new_sources.citation: Alex Callinicos, review of Bryan D. Palmer, Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (Philadelphia: Temple University Press, 1990), Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992): 311–313. doi:10.2307/25143611.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF of the issue's reviews section (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/4845; running heads 312, 313; signed Alex Callinicos, University of York (GB)); Crossref gives volume 29, first page 311. Two-column text, reassembled column by column. Quotations of Palmer with Callinicos's page references to the book: xiii, 25, 138, 139, 189, 199, 209–11, 216–17. His own judgements: the results are 'admirable'; disagreements 'relatively minor'; Palmer 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received' (p. 312); 'underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action'; Palmer 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (p. 313).

new_sources.scope_note: An in-period Marxist review of Descent into Discourse that quotes it with page numbers.

verification.note: Chapter read in full, with its 81 notes, on AU Press Digital Publications (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; the web edition has no page numbers). Volume metadata from Crossref (editors Carleton, McCoy and Smith; Athabasca University Press; published 31 May 2021) and the volume's introduction, read. A later reading (2021) by a historian of Georgian England. Used: Palmer's 1993 Left History interview, 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Givertz and Klee, Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted); A Culture in Conflict quoting Thompson's culture as a 'way of struggle' (pp. xii, xiv, as cited); The Making as 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation; Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position' but not 'a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism'; Thompson's 'rejection of economic determinism and the base–superstructure model of explanation favoured by many Marxists'; Descent into Discourse on Scott (pp. 81–85, 180, as cited); Palmer's 1993 concession that poststructurally inclined historians 'rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted). Rogers's note 26 dates Kaye and McClelland's E. P. Thompson: Critical Perspectives to 1980; Crossref's 1992 ILWCH review of that volume suggests c. 1990.

cdnsrc_palmer_1990.note: Book still unread for the 1.134 person entry (Internet Archive descentintodisco00palm and two other copies are borrow-only; search-inside returned HTTP 403). Open Library OL3089393W confirms Temple University Press, 1990. In-period reviews located through Crossref: Thomas Bender, Journal of Social History 25:2 (1991): 407–408; David Hollinger, Journal of American History (1991); Allan G. Bogue, American Historical Review 96:5 (1991); Jack Amariglio, Journal of Economic History (1991); Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992): 311–313 (read; pe134_palmer_callinicos_1992); Reimer, Canadian Journal of History 27:1 (1992). Only Callinicos was read. Its pages are quoted in the 1.134 draft as Callinicos (xiii, 25, 138, 139, 189, 199, 209–11, 216–17) and, as later readings, Rogers and Pearson (2021: pp. 79, 81–85, 172, 180, 183, 186) cite them.

wcreq_bercuson_1981.note: Pp. 95–97 and 107–108 re-read for the 1.134 person entry in the PDF on the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658). p. 96: the new labour history's method 'as Palmer describes it' ('sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past'; 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research'; n. 10: A Culture in Conflict, xii–xiv) and 'what Palmer labels "a tradition of empirical Marxism"' (n. 11: xiii). p. 97: 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (n. 13: xii). pp. 107–108: 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107); 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108).

lof_palmer_2009.note: Re-read in full for the 1.134 person entry (Carleton Underhill Review page, Fall 2009, 'Feature Review Essay'; unpaginated). Added to the earlier note: liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism'; past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order"'; the full sentence 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression'; the qualification 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself'; Reasoning Otherwise 'stands as an undeniable achievement'.

pl129_palmer_1993_homage.note: Both parts downloaded from the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/4897 and /4917) for the 1.134 drafts, searched in full and read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18. Part I, p. 68: Thompson's socialist humanism against Stalinism, 'governed as it was by anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'; 'In the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor, all of humanity's being could be reduced to a mere reflection of the economic substance of society'; n. 64 cites 'Socialist Humanism' and 'Agency and Choice' and Palmer's own Making of E.P. Thompson, 48–51. Part II, p. 17: The Making as 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' in which 'the creation of the working class was that of a determined process: steam power plus the factory system equals the working class', quoting Thompson from interviews (n. 9 lists Hogben 1988, Scott 1980 and the Visions of History interview; not read). Part II, p. 18: 'the historian has got to be listening all the time'. A Thompson admirer's in-period reading (1993–94), not Thompson's own text.
